summaries.example: Imagine hearing a bell and seeing it at the same time. Yogācāra thinkers asked how many parts of the mind work together in one moment. They suggested that different kinds of awareness can happen together, while another part of the mind quietly carries habits and memories forward.
summaries.summary: Yogācāra is a wide-ranging tradition of Mahāyāna Buddhist philosophy that began in India. Its name connects yoga with practice, discipline, or meditation. Yogācāra thinkers were especially interested in how consciousness works and how the mind can be changed on the path to liberation. They described eight kinds of consciousness. Six are ordinary kinds connected with the senses and thinking. A seventh, the defiled mind, helps explain why people cling to an idea of a permanent self. An eighth, the store consciousness, was described as a hidden stream that carries seeds or tendencies from actions and experiences. These seeds help explain habits, future experiences, bodily life, and karmic continuity without saying that there is an everlasting soul. Yogācāra is also known for the mind-only or cognition-only teaching. This teaching gives mind an important role in explaining the world we experience. Some versions say that perceived objects are only appearances in cognition; other interpretations are more cautious. The tradition also developed the three-natures teaching: things seem to have a separate, solid form, they arise through causes and conditions, and their deeper nature is understood when mistaken divisions between self and object are seen through. Yogācāra included several important texts and figures, such as Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, Dignāga, and Dharmakīrti. It was not a single unchanging system, but a diverse family of ideas.
key_ideas: Yogācāra began in India and became one of the major philosophical traditions of Mahāyāna Buddhism.
Its name is linked with practice, especially meditation and training the mind.
Yogācāra described eight kinds of consciousness instead of the six used in an older Buddhist model.
The store consciousness was used to explain how habits, actions, rebirth, and personal continuity could continue without an unchanging soul.
Some Yogācāra thinkers argued that objects depend on cognition, but scholars disagree about exactly how strong this claim is.
The tradition had many teachers, texts, branches, and later developments in China, Japan, Tibet, and elsewhere in Asia.
summaries.why_it_matters: Yogācāra matters because it offers a detailed way to think about attention, habits, identity, perception, and change. It also shows how a philosophical tradition can connect careful reasoning with meditation and the goal of liberation. Its questions about whether we experience things directly or through mental appearances still sound familiar today.

important_terms.definition: A major philosophical tradition of Mahāyāna Buddhism that studied meditation, consciousness, and the path to liberation.
The idea that what we experience depends deeply on mind or awareness. It does not have exactly one agreed meaning.
A continuing, hidden stream of awareness said to hold seeds, or tendencies, left by actions and experiences.
A part of the mind connected with mistaken ideas about a permanent “I.”
The idea that actions can leave effects that appear later.
A person’s mistaken picture of things as separate, solid, and independent, especially a self and outside objects.

questions_to_think_about: Can a person change while still having a sense of being the same person?
Could habits be compared to tiny seeds that grow when the right conditions arrive?
If two people see the same event, what might explain their having similar experiences?
Why might meditation help someone notice mistaken ideas about the self?

summaries.example: Suppose several people watch a kettle boil. They seem to share one object in one place, yet each person has a distinct experience. A Yogācāra philosopher might ask whether the kettle must be an independently existing material thing, or whether shared karmic conditions and mental seeds can explain why similar appearances arise for different minds. This is not a simple claim that “nothing exists”; it is part of a debate about what cognition reveals and what ultimately exists.
summaries.summary: Yogācāra is a historically extensive and philosophically diverse tradition of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism. Its name is associated with practice and mental cultivation, and its works connect theories of consciousness with the path to liberation. The tradition is especially associated with Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, whose writings systematized major doctrines, and with Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, who developed a closely related logico-epistemological tradition. The older Buddhist model recognized six consciousnesses: five sensory forms and mental consciousness. Yogācāra added the kliṣṭamanas, a subliminal process that appropriates the ālayavijñāna as a self, and the ālayavijñāna, a continuous store or substratum consciousness. Karmic seeds in this stream were used to explain habits, the reappearance of consciousness, personal continuity, and continuity across rebirth, while the store consciousness itself was said to be changing and to cease with liberation. The most debated Yogācāra doctrine is cittamātra or vijñaptimātra. It can be read as saying that objects are appearances within cognition, that perceptions arise from mental causes, or more strongly that no mind-independent material world exists. These are not identical claims. The three-natures doctrine clarifies the issue: the imagined nature is the apparent division into independent subjects and objects; the dependent nature is the causal flow on which appearances rely; and the perfected nature is the realization of the absence of the imagined division from that flow. Vasubandhu defended mind-only against arguments from spatial order, shared experience, and practical effects, using dreams and other cases where appearances occur without ordinary external objects. Dignāga and Dharmakīrti offered further arguments about the form
key_ideas: Yogācāra developed in India within Mahāyāna Buddhism and influenced Buddhist thought across Asia.

The tradition’s sources include the Yogācārabhūmi, the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, and works attributed to Asaṅga and Vasubandhu; the dates and authorship of some texts remain uncertain.
Classical Yogācāra expanded the older six-consciousness model by adding the defiled mind and the store consciousness.
The store consciousness explains how karmic seeds can preserve continuity without becoming a permanent self; Yogācāra compares it to a changing river rather than an eternal substance.

The mind-only debate has several levels: what objects are perceived, what causes perceptions, and what is ultimately real. Interpretations range from epistemological idealism to ontological idealism or phenomenological readings.

Dignāga and Dharmakīrti developed logical and epistemological arguments about perception, representation, self-awareness, and other minds, while later thinkers disagreed about whether Yogācāra ultimately accepts other minds.
summaries.why_it_matters: Yogācāra matters to philosophy because it treats consciousness not as a minor topic but as central to metaphysics, epistemology, psychology, and ethics. Its analysis asks what perception gives us, how representations relate to objects, how a person remains responsible while lacking a permanent self, and whether belief in other minds can be justified. The disagreements within Yogācāra also caution against treating a large historical tradition as one simple doctrine.

important_terms.definition: One of the two major philosophical traditions of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism, focused especially on consciousness, meditation, and liberation.
A teaching often translated as “mind-only” or “cognition-only,” giving mind or cognition priority in explaining perceived reality; its precise metaphysical force is disputed.
The subliminal stream of consciousness said to contain karmic seeds and to support continuity across changing experiences and lives.
A continuously operating form of consciousness associated with self-grasping, self-delusion, self-conceit, and self-love.
The view that mental access is limited to appearances or contents in cognition, without necessarily denying a mind-independent reality.
The stronger view that mind or mental states are fundamental and that a material world independent of mind does not exist.
Yogācāra’s framework of imagined, dependent, and perfected natures, used to analyze appearance, causation, and insight into reality.
A position denying that other minds exist, or, in an epistemological form, denying that their existence can be known.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining an experience through mental causes show that external objects do not exist, or only that we do not directly know them?
Can a changing stream of mental events explain personal responsibility better than an unchanging self?
What would count as evidence for the existence of another mind?
How does the three-natures model distinguish ordinary appearance from deeper understanding?
Why might a Buddhist philosopher reject both a permanent self and the conclusion that only one mind exists?

summaries.example: Think about learning to play a song. At first, each note takes effort. After much practice, your fingers seem to know what to do. A Yogācāra explanation might describe this as a tendency formed by earlier actions. The tradition used the idea of stored “seeds” to explain how past actions can shape later thoughts and experiences, while still denying that an unchanging soul carries them.
summaries.summary: Yogācāra is a large and varied tradition of Mahāyāna Buddhist philosophy that arose in India and later influenced Buddhist thought in China, Japan, Tibet, and other parts of Asia. Its name is connected with practice, discipline, and meditation. Yogācāra philosophers wanted to understand how consciousness works and how changing the mind can lead toward liberation. Their model of the mind was more complex than an older model with six consciousnesses. They added a defiled mind, which quietly supports our tendency to think there is a permanent “me,” and a store consciousness, which continues beneath ordinary thoughts and perceptions. The store consciousness was said to contain karmic seeds. These are not physical seeds, but potential effects left by actions and experiences. They help explain why habits and experiences can continue without an eternal soul. Yogācāra is also linked with the mind-only or cognition-only teaching. This teaching says that mind has an important priority in explaining what we experience. Some philosophers understood it strongly, as a denial of independently existing material objects. Others understood it more cautiously, as a claim that we directly encounter only mental appearances and cannot simply assume that perception reveals objects exactly as they are. The three-natures teaching helps explain this. The imagined nature is our ordinary mistake of treating subjects and objects as fully separate. The dependent nature is the flow of experiences produced by causes and conditions. The perfected nature is insight into the absence of that mistaken separation. Important figures included Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, Dignāga, and Dharmakīrti, and their followers did not agree on every point.
key_ideas: Yogācāra began in India as one of two major Mahāyāna philosophical traditions, alongside Madhyamaka.
The name suggests practice and mental training, and the tradition connected meditation with understanding reality.
Its thinkers proposed eight kinds of consciousness: six familiar forms, plus the defiled mind and store consciousness.
The store consciousness was meant to explain how karma and personal continuity work even though Buddhism rejects a permanent self.
The mind-only teaching led to disagreement: some readings deny mind-independent objects, while others say only that we know mental appearances directly.
The three natures describe how things seem, how they arise through conditions, and how insight corrects mistaken divisions between subject and object.
summaries.why_it_matters: Yogācāra matters because it connects everyday questions about identity and habit with larger questions about reality and knowledge. It asks whether seeing is simply receiving information from outside or involves active mental construction. It also shows how philosophers can disagree within one tradition while sharing concerns about suffering, responsibility, meditation, and liberation.

important_terms.definition: A Mahāyāna Buddhist philosophical tradition that studied the mind, meditation, perception, and liberation.
A label for teachings that say experience depends on mind or cognition; different Yogācāra texts and scholars explain this differently.
A hidden, continuing level of consciousness said to preserve karmic seeds and support the flow of experience.
A layer of mind that mistakes the ongoing flow of experience for a permanent self.
A potential left by an action or experience that may later produce a thought, habit, or perception.
The mistaken appearance that there are completely independent selves and objects.
The idea that something is empty of a separate existence because it depends on causes and conditions.
A philosophical problem about whether and how we can know that other people have minds.

questions_to_think_about: If your habits change over time, what makes them connected to your earlier actions?
Does a dream show that an experience can seem real without an ordinary outside object?
When you see a friend act kindly, how might you reason that your friend has thoughts and feelings?
Can something be real in everyday life but not ultimately separate or independent?
Why would a tradition interested in meditation also study logic and perception?
